rulings.matter: 1 -- is CHA-0001 upheld, and how far does the upholding reach
rulings.ruling: UPHELD IN FULL, ON BOTH CLAUSES. The arithmetic was verified independently before this adjudication was dispatched and I did not re-derive it: at magnitude 1e8 the binade is [2^26, 2^27), ulp is 8, half-ulp is 4, an increment of 2 is fully absorbed, and 1f - 1e8f + 2f is bit-identical to 1f - 1e8f in binary32. Criterion 11's stated justification -- that each iteration 'strictly increases' the field -- is false for binary32 addition, and with the default fixture Scheduler(firstDelay: 1f, interval: 2f) the call Tick(1e8f, buffer) enters the loop at WaveScheduler.cs:70 and does not leave it, calling into.Add on every iteration. Criterion 11's second clause, that the invariant be STATED somewhere in the delivered code or tests, is also unmet: nothing in Assets/Core or Assets/Tests states it. I record what the upholding does NOT reach, because an over-broad upholding is as damaging as a dismissal. It does not reach the shipped Unity build: Assets/Unity/EnemySpawner.cs:45 passes Time.deltaTime, which is never 1e8, and qa-director said so unprompted rather than inflating the finding, which is the reason this challenge was cheap to adjudicate. It does not reach WO-0010's other sixteen criteria, which I adopt from RUL-0002 rather than re-deriving. It does not reach the implementer's competence: the bounded-buffer harness at WaveSchedulerTests.cs:38 is good engineering, criterion 11 was written by the order's author and not by the implementer, and an implementer who satisfies a criterion's letter while its stated justification is arithmetically false has been misled by the specification, not merely careless. The finding is against the delivery, and the specification carries a share of it.

rulings.matter: 2 -- the remedy: option (a), option (b), or a third way
rulings.ruling:
NEITHER AS PUT. I rule a third way, and I will give the reasoning for rejecting each named option first because the rejection of (b) is the precedent-setting part.

OPTION (b) -- amend criterion 11 to the dt range over which the current loop provably terminates -- IS REFUSED, on three independent grounds, any one of which would be sufficient.

First, the criterion is satisfiable. qa-director's own note is decisive: an implementation exists that satisfies criterion 11 exactly as written, so this is a defect against the criterion and not a defect in the criterion. Amending a satisfiable criterion because the delivered code does not satisfy it is narrowing a claim to fit an implementation. That is not on the forbidden-remedies list -- a criterion is not a test assertion -- but it is the same motion as weakening an assertion, and this is the first challenge this studio has ever run end to end. Whatever I do here becomes the template. If challenge number one is settled by rewriting the claim to match the code, every future challenge has a cheap exit and the mechanism is decorative within a month.

Second, and more concretely, an amended criterion 11 would be precisely statable but not usefully checkable, and it would certify a region that is not safe. The threshold depends on _interval as well as dt: full absorption begins at |timer| >= 2^25 x _interval, with a round-half-to-even grey zone from 2^24 x _interval, so the honest statement is a conditional relation between two runtime values with a fuzzy edge, not a property of the type. It cannot be checked by inspection, and a test of it must pick arbitrary intervals and stay clear of the grey edge, which means the amended criterion would be verified nowhere near its own boundary. Worse, the ratio that triggers absorption is the same ratio that determines the spawn count: the loop appends dt/_interval items, so absorption cannot occur below roughly 2^24 due spawns. An amended criterion 11 would therefore certify as 'terminating' calls that append sixteen million or more SpawnRequests into the caller's buffer in one call. That is a hang and an out-of-memory in every practical sense. Option (b) does not narrow the claim to a safe region; it narrows it to a region that is merely finite.

Third, ADR-0001. Core is engine-free for exactly one reason: so the game can be run headless, deterministically, thousands of times without a licence. The harness that does this, Studio/sim/MergeSurvivor.Sim/Program.cs, chooses its own dt at Program.cs:224-239 and is the studio's primary verification instrument. Stated without inflation: it does not hit this today, because RunSchedule is called only with 1f/30f, 1f/60f and 1f/240f, and no existing caller anywhere passes a dt near the threshold. The hazard is latent, not live. But the threshold for the sim's own configuration, SpawnInterval 2f, is dt of roughly 3.4e7 seconds, and a sweep over a year of simulated time in coarse steps is within a factor of two of that -- not an absurd future choice for a balance harness. When it is reached, the symptom is an unattended overnight run that never returns, diagnosed as 'the sim hung' rather than as an absorbed increment. A Core method that does not return on an input the harness may legitimately choose bears directly on the property ADR-0001 exists to protect, and unclaiming it in prose does not make the harness safer.

OPTION (a) AS FORMULATED -- compute the number of due spawns arithmetically instead of iterating -- IS ALSO REFUSED, on cost and risk, which is the founder's own framing and it holds. Replacing repeated float accumulation with a computed count changes the arithmetic on EVERY dt, not only the pathological ones. Repeated addition and a ceiling division do not agree in the last ulp: for a timer at -0.3 and an interval of 0.1 the iterative path and the divide-and-ceiling path can differ by one spawn, and the divergence surface includes the existing 0.3f two-step sequence test and, more expensively, G4's determinism and frame-rate-independence metrics in Program.cs. The count would also need computing in a type that cannot overflow, since dt/_interval exceeds int range for small intervals. So option (a) buys termination at the price of a real regression risk across every spawn in the game, and still appends the same fifty million items for dt = 1e8. It is the expensive remedy and it does not remove the allocation.

WHAT I RULE INSTEAD -- option (c), reject the input the schedule cannot advance through, detected exactly rather than by threshold. WaveScheduler.Tick must determine, BEFORE mutating _timeUntilNextSpawn and before appending anything, what the timer value would be after subtracting dt, and whether adding _interval to that value yields a value strictly greater than it. If a spawn is due (the post-subtraction value is at or below zero) and that addition does not strictly increase it, the method rejects dt: it throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException naming dt, leaves _timeUntilNextSpawn exactly as it was, and appends nothing -- the same throwing-path contract criterion 2 already imposes on the DtGuard path. Requirements on the shape of the fix, which are not negotiable by the implementer: (i) the check is the direct non-progress comparison, not a hard-coded threshold constant -- nobody should ever have to re-derive 2^24 x _interval, and a constant would be wrong for a different _interval; (ii) the check lives in WaveScheduler.Tick, NOT in DtGuard, because it is a scheduler-specific relation between dt and _interval and folding it into the shared dt guard would conflate two different defect classes at exactly the moment WO-0011 is generalising that helper; (iii) the exception message must state the predicate actually enforced, in the manner PRO-0002 and criterion 12 require -- that dt is too large relative to the spawn interval for the schedule to advance -- and must not reuse DtGuard's message, which states a different predicate; (iv) no change to PlayerMotor, which this challenge does not touch.

WHY (c) BEATS BOTH. Behaviour is provably identical to today for every input on which today's code returns, because the only added path fires precisely when the first increment fails to increase the timer, which today means the loop never terminates -- so there is no dt with defined behaviour today whose behaviour changes, and the G4 metrics cannot move. The soundness argument is short enough to state in the doc comment and check: the timer rises monotonically toward zero, so its magnitude is non-increasing across iterations, so its ulp is non-increasing, so progress at the first step implies progress at every step; the loop therefore terminates in a finite number of iterations for every dt the method accepts. That makes criterion 11's universal claim TRUE rather than narrower -- no dt reaches the loop and fails to terminate it. And, unlike (b), it removes the hazard instead of unclaiming it: after (c) there exists no finite input on which WaveScheduler.Tick fails to return.

I record the honest cost of (c), since it is the one thing (a) would have done better: it requires a small consequential amendment to criterion 11, addressed in matter 3. I judge that acceptable because of the direction of the amendment -- see there.
authorises: WaveScheduler.Tick may reject a finite, non-negative dt by throwing ArgumentOutOfRangeException when the resulting timer cannot be advanced by _interval in binary32. This is a change to the Tick contract and would otherwise contradict criterion 11 as currently written and trip WO-0010's escalateIf clause about callers depending on Tick's acceptance; it is authorised here, and the implementer may treat this ruling as the authorisation.
work-order-author may amend WO-0010 acceptance criterion 11, in the terms set out in matter 3 of this ruling and in no others.

rulings.matter: 3 -- the consequential amendment to criterion 11, its direction, and who may make it
rulings.ruling:
AMENDED IN ITS JUSTIFICATION AND ITS DESCRIPTION OF THE ACCEPTED INPUT SET, NOT IN ITS SAFETY CLAIM. I am aware this looks like the option (b) I just refused, so I will draw the line precisely, because the line is the whole ruling. Option (b) amends the SAFETY CLAIM: it says the loop terminates over a narrower range of dt, and leaves in existence dt values on which Tick does not return. My amendment leaves the safety claim universal and strengthens it -- after the fix, NO finite input causes Tick to fail to return -- and amends only two things that the fix makes factually inaccurate: the parenthetical assertion that the accepted set is every finite dt >= 0 however large, and the justification clause that appeals to binary32 addition strictly increasing its left operand, which is false and must not survive in the record as though it were true. One narrows what is promised while the hazard stays; the other removes the hazard and corrects a false sentence about what is promised. Those are not the same act.

The amended criterion 11 must assert, and be checkable on, all four of the following: (1) for every dt WaveScheduler.Tick accepts without throwing, the loop terminates in a finite number of iterations -- unrestricted, no dt range; (2) the justification, stated correctly: the method rejects, before mutating state or appending anything, any dt for which adding _interval to the post-subtraction timer would not strictly increase it, and since the timer's magnitude is non-increasing across iterations, progress at the first step implies progress at every step; (3) the rejected set is exactly the inputs for which the schedule cannot advance, determined by direct comparison and not by a threshold constant; (4) the method does NOT over-reject -- a large finite dt on which the schedule can still advance is accepted and produces the full catch-up count. Clause (4) is the one I insist on hardest and it is the direct application of the standing correction qa-director issued in RUL-0002 matter 2: asked 'what implementation makes this criterion false', the answer for a naive fix is 'one that rejects everything above some conservative constant', and clause (4) plus its test is what catches that. Criterion 11's second clause is unchanged and still binds: the invariant must be STATED, in Tick's XML doc comment and pinned by a test, not merely be true.

Procedure, which matters as much as the content. The amendment is work-order-author's act, on this instruction, and mine to authorise but not to perform. It must carry a rationale citing RUL-0003 and CHA-0001. The original text of criterion 11 must be preserved in the record -- in CHA-0001 it already is -- so that anyone reading later can see what changed and satisfy themselves it was strengthened rather than fitted to the code. No other criterion of WO-0010 may be touched under this authorisation.

rulings.matter: 4 -- the ratchet, and a defect in the ratchet as proposed
rulings.ruling:
THE RATCHET IS REQUIRED, AND THE FORM PROPOSED FOR IT IS WRONG IN A WAY THAT WOULD HAVE FAILED SILENTLY. qa-director's proposed regression test is: assert that Scheduler(firstDelay: 1f, interval: 2f).Tick(1e8f, new BoundedSpawnRequestBuffer()) 'completes and returns a finite count'. As an assertion of completion-with-a-count that test does not pass after ANY of the three candidate remedies. The bounded buffer's cap is 1000 (WaveSchedulerTests.cs:38). At dt = 1e8 and interval 2f, fifty million spawns are genuinely due, so under option (a)'s arithmetic count the call still blows the cap and still throws BoundedBufferCapacityExceededException -- red before the change and red after it, which is a ratchet that never goes green and would have been 'fixed' by widening the cap, which is a forbidden remedy in all but name. This is not a criticism of the finding; it is a consequence of the fact, established in matter 2, that absorption cannot occur below roughly 2^24 due spawns, so no absorbing case can also be a small-buffer case. It is the reason the ratchet must be specified by the order author against the chosen remedy rather than lifted verbatim from the challenge.

Under the remedy I have ruled, the ratchet becomes clean and cheap, and qa-director's harness is exactly right for it. Required tests, all in Assets/Tests/Core.Tests and none of them mine to write: (i) Scheduler(firstDelay: 1f, interval: 2f).Tick(1e8f, boundedBuffer) throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException naming dt; the buffer is empty afterwards; a subsequent Tick with a normal dt spawns exactly as if the rejected call had never happened. Against the pre-fix code this fails fast and deterministically with BoundedBufferCapacityExceededException at 1000 appends -- red, in milliseconds, not a hang -- and passes after. That is the ratchet. (ii) The non-over-rejection test required by amended criterion 11 clause (4): a large finite dt that is still well below the absorption relation -- a value on the order of 1e5 seconds at interval 2f -- is ACCEPTED and returns the full catch-up count, appending every due spawn. Without (ii) the ratchet is satisfiable by an implementation that rejects any large dt, which would be a second defect wearing the fix's clothes. (iii) The stated-invariant requirement of criterion 11 clause two, pinned by a test rather than only asserted in a comment.

Evidence. T0/T1 as WO-0010 already requires, showing each new test's actual pre-fix failure output rather than an assertion that it would fail -- the same gap RUL-0001 recorded against WO-0008 criterion 7 and RUL-0002 recorded again here; it is now twice in a row and I am not willing to see it a third time. Additionally, and this is new: because the remedy touches spawn scheduling, the evidence must include a T3 run of Studio/sim/MergeSurvivor.Sim with the pre-change and post-change trees at the same seed, with the resulting metrics.json compared field by field. My soundness argument in matter 2 says those metrics cannot move; that argument is worth exactly as much as the run that confirms it, and the run is cheap. If any metric moves, the implementer stops and escalates rather than adjusting anything -- a moved metric would mean my monotonicity reasoning is wrong, which is a fact I would want to learn immediately.

rulings.matter: 5 -- sequencing against WO-0011, the approved systemic sweep
rulings.ruling:
NOT INSIDE WO-0011, AND NOT A NEW ORDER EITHER: THE REMEDY IS CARRIED UNDER WO-0010, WHICH STAYS OPEN UNTIL IT IS MET, AND IS DISPATCHED AHEAD OF WO-0011 WITH EXCLUSIVE USE OF THE FILE.

Against folding it into WO-0011, three reasons, in ascending order of importance. (i) Coupling: WO-0010 is sixteen criteria from done and WO-0011 is a seven-instance sweep that does not exist as a file yet. Folding the remedy into the sweep means WO-0010's gate cannot be reached until the sweep's is, which is how a nearly-finished order gets held hostage by a large one. (ii) File contention: WO-0011 edits the constructor guards at WaveScheduler.cs:29, 35 and 41 while this remedy edits Tick in the same file. Running them concurrently reproduces exactly the problem that already cost this round its scope evidence -- RUL-0002's limitations record that two agents ran concurrently and check-write-scope.sh diffs the whole tree against HEAD, so nothing this round could be attributed. Do not pay that cost twice in three days. (iii) Decisive: THEY ARE NOT THE SAME DEFECT. WO-0011's family is 'NaN passes an ordering comparison, so a guard does not enforce the predicate its message states'. CHA-0001 is 'binary32 addition is not strictly increasing, so a loop that looks like it makes progress does not'. There is no NaN anywhere in CHA-0001; every value in it is finite. The G2 check WO-0011 adds to stop an eleventh instance -- whatever form it takes, presumably flagging comparison-based float guards that omit a finiteness test -- would NOT have caught this one and must never be credited with covering it. Filing them together would record the studio as believing eight instances share one root cause when it is seven plus one, and would inflate what the new G2 check is understood to protect against. That is a taxonomy error, and taxonomy errors are how a defect class gets marked closed while an instance walks free -- the precise failure PRO-0005 and PRO-0006 have each had to point out once already.

Against minting a new order: the unmet criterion belongs to WO-0010, WO-0010 is dispatched and not complete, the remedy sits inside its existing writeScope of Assets/Core/** and Assets/Tests/Core.Tests/**, its retryBudget of 3 and its T0/T1 evidence requirement already apply, and its own goal sentence already names the unbounded loop as the thing it exists to eliminate. Opening a separate order for a criterion of an order still in flight would let WO-0010 be recorded as closed on sixteen of seventeen criteria with the seventeenth living somewhere else -- 'recorded as closed when it was not' is the exact failure this studio keeps catching, and I will not introduce a bookkeeping shape that produces it. So: same order, one gate, one verdict, covering all seventeen criteria including the amended eleventh.

Dispatch order and interlock: the WO-0010 remedy goes first and alone. WO-0011 must not be dispatched against Assets/Core/Spawning/WaveScheduler.cs until the remedy is merged and WO-0010's gate has ruled. WO-0011 may be authored and reviewed in parallel -- authoring costs nothing and contends with nothing -- but its dispatch waits. If the sweep's author judges the wait material to the founder's schedule, that comes to me and not to the founder; on the evidence in front of me it is a delay of one order, not of a release.

One consequence for the record: upholding a challenge requires a resultingTaskId, and here it is WO-0010 itself, since the corrective work is carried under the order whose criterion was violated. CHA-0001 should be set to status 'upheld', with this ruling's id and ruledAt recorded and resultingTaskId 'WO-0010'. If a kernel cross-check refuses a resultingTaskId equal to the challenged order's taskId, that is a gap in the contract rather than a reason to change the ruling: in that case mint a corrective order at the next free id, scope it to this remedy alone, and record WO-0010 as blocked on it -- the sequencing above is unchanged either way, and the gap should come back to me as a proposal.

rulings.matter: 6 -- what this remedy does not fix, and where that goes
rulings.ruling:
IT FIXES NON-TERMINATION AND NOT UNBOUNDED ALLOCATION, AND I WILL NOT LET THAT DIFFERENCE BE BLURRED IN THE DIGEST. After the fix, a dt of 1e6 seconds at interval 2f is still accepted -- correctly, since the schedule genuinely advances -- and still appends five hundred thousand SpawnRequests into the caller's buffer in one call, and a dt just under the rejection relation still appends on the order of sixteen million. That is finite, defined and reproducible, which is a real improvement over a loop that never returns, and it is emphatically not safe for an unattended harness. Capping catch-up is a decision about what a long hitch should produce, which belongs to the game designer and not to engineering, to quality, or to me acting unasked -- PRO-0006's note (b) reached that conclusion first and correctly, and logged it rather than inflating it into work. Logging it was right for a quality director. Leaving it logged is not right for me: routing questions to the division that owns them is the job. I have therefore raised PRO-0007 to put the catch-up ceiling to design as a decision request, referencing PRO-0006 note (b) rather than re-deriving it.

Interaction between the two, stated now so nobody has to work it out later: a per-call spawn ceiling, if design adopts one, would subsume this remedy -- a bounded loop cannot fail to terminate regardless of what the arithmetic does. I still rule the remedy first rather than waiting, because the hazard is live in the tree today and the design answer is not, and because the remedy is provably behaviour-preserving whereas a ceiling is not. But if a ceiling is later adopted, replacing this remedy's rejection contract with it would change the ratchet test from matter 4(i) from 'throws' to 'returns the ceiling', which is a replacement of a passing assertion and requires written authorisation under L-002 at that time. It is not authorised here, and PRO-0007 must say so.

rulings.matter: 7 -- what must survive this round, given the mechanism ran for the first time
rulings.ruling:
THE CHALLENGE MECHANISM WORKED AND I AM RECORDING WHY, BECAUSE ONE SUCCESSFUL RUN IS NOT YET A HABIT. Three things earned their cost here and should be repeated verbatim. First, qa-director stated reachability without inflation -- naming that EnemySpawner cannot reach this, and that the finding is about the criterion rather than a shipped hang -- which is the single reason this adjudication was cheap: I did not have to discount the claim before weighing it, and an adjudicator who has to discount claims stops reading them. Second, the challenge explicitly declined to choose the remedy, calling it engineering's and the author's. That is the correct boundary and it is why there was a decision left for me to take rather than a fait accompli to ratify. Third, the challenge named its own falsifier and undertook to withdraw if execution contradicted the derivation. That is what made the arithmetic verifiable in minutes.

One lesson is durable enough to leave the round, and I direct it be recorded as L-003, worded to be usable rather than admired: 'A criterion phrased as a universal claim must name the arithmetic it depends on, and floating-point accumulation is not the arithmetic it looks like. Repeated addition into a float field is not strictly increasing: once the addend falls below half an ulp of the accumulator the store rounds back to the identical bit pattern and the loop makes no progress. Any termination argument of the form each iteration increases X by a fixed positive amount is false as stated whenever X is a float, and must be replaced either by a direct non-progress check or by an argument that bounds the accumulator's magnitude. Promotion candidate: a G2 analyzer flagging a loop whose only progress toward its exit condition is a compound assignment to a floating-point field.' LESSONS.md is not mine to write; this goes to whoever owns lesson promotion, and CHA-0001's lessonRecorded flag should be set true only once it is actually there. Note also for that owner: L-003 is a DIFFERENT lesson from the one WO-0011's G2 check encodes, for the reason given in matter 5, and the two must not be merged into one entry.

Finally, on RUL-0002's standing correction -- that the named-wrong-implementation discipline applies first to every criterion phrased as a universal quantifier. It is well reasoned, it is the instrument that found this, and it is within quality's own authority to issue. It is not mine to endorse or to soften and I do neither, beyond observing that I have applied it to my own directive in matter 3 clause (4), which is the honest test of whether one believes a rule.

criteriaAssessment.notes: This assessment is ADOPTED from RUL-0002, not independently re-derived: I adjudicated CHA-0001, which concerns criterion 11 only, and re-grading sixteen criteria the quality director graded three days ago would be duplicated cost with no new information. Criterion 11 is violated and stays violated until the remedy in matter 2 is delivered, criterion 11 is amended per matter 3, and the ratchet in matter 4 is green with its evidence filed. I deliberately do NOT record criterion 11 as unsatisfiableAsWritten: it is satisfiable as written -- an implementation accepting every finite dt and terminating would satisfy it -- and recording it as unsatisfiable would be the schema-shaped version of the option (b) I refused, converting a defect against the criterion into a defect in the criterion. The amendment I authorise in matter 3 is consequential to the remedy, not a concession that the criterion could not be met. Criteria 15 and 17 remain unevidenced for want of an evidence record under Studio/evidence, which is the second consecutive round this has occurred; it is a process failure rather than a code failure and matter 4 restates it as blocking.

Scheduler-specific and therefore in WaveScheduler.cs, not in DtGuard. Full terms in matter 2.

Criterion 11 amended by work-order-author on the terms of matter 3, asserting the unrestricted termination claim, the corrected justification, the exact rejection relation, and the non-over-rejection clause; with rationale citing RUL-0003 and CHA-0001 and the original text preserved.
Criterion 11 second clause: the invariant must be STATED in Tick's XML doc comment and pinned by a test. It is stated nowhere today.

Ratchet test: Scheduler(firstDelay: 1f, interval: 2f).Tick(1e8f, boundedBuffer) throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException, buffer empty, subsequent Tick unaffected. Must be demonstrated red pre-fix with its actual output (BoundedBufferCapacityExceededException at the 1000 cap) and green post-fix. The form proposed in CHA-0001 -- 'completes and returns a finite count' -- must NOT be used; see matter 4 for why it can never go green.

All blocking conditions of RUL-0002 stand unaltered and are carried forward in full: criterion 17's T0/T1 pre-fix failure output for each new regression test; criterion 15's warnings-as-errors build and full green run, attributable to a tree with no other agent's work in flight; the git diff of WaveSchedulerTests.cs and PlayerMotorTests.cs confirming the eighteen original assertions are untouched; and quality's directed message-equality test across the three Tick methods. I neither cleared nor weakened any of them and have no standing to.
G2 must pass on its own terms. Nothing in this ruling touches it, no part of it is overridden, and no verdict on WO-0010 is given here -- this ruling adjudicates a challenge and does not sign a gate.

boundariesObserved: I wrote no production code and no test code, and no file under Assets/** was touched by this adjudication. I described the required behaviour of the remedy in prose and named the tests that must exist; writing them is engineering's and quality's, and every one of them is dispatched rather than performed. I did not amend criterion 11 or any other acceptance criterion: matter 3 instructs work-order-author to amend it and states the terms and the limits of that authorisation, and WO-0010's acceptanceCriteria array is exactly as its author left it. I did not mark WO-0010 complete, did not sign or pre-empt any gate, and gave no verdict on G2 -- the verdict field here records the state of criterion 11 under CHA-0001, not a gate outcome. I cleared, weakened and reordered none of RUL-0002's blocking conditions; they are carried forward verbatim in substance, including the ones that constrain quality's own division. I did not re-derive the sixteen criteria outside the challenge, and said so rather than implying a fuller review than I performed. I did not re-litigate the arithmetic, which was settled before dispatch. I did not edit CHA-0001's status, Studio/orders, LESSONS.md, the constitution, CI or Studio/build; where those need changing I named the change and its owner. I did not escalate to the founder, because nothing here touches the pillars, the non-goals, an irreversible action, monetisation or player data, and no two bosses are deadlocked -- this is a first-round adjudication of a single challenge and settling it internally is the point of the role.
limitations: I have no shell and ran nothing. Three consequences, stated rather than glossed. First, my central technical claim -- that the non-progress check leaves behaviour identical for every input on which today's code returns -- is a monotonicity argument, not an observation: the timer rises toward zero, so its magnitude is non-increasing, so its ulp is non-increasing, so progress at the first step implies progress at every step. I believe it is sound and I have made it falsifiable by requiring the pre/post metrics.json comparison in matter 4; if any metric moves, my reasoning is wrong and I want to be told immediately rather than have anyone reconcile the difference. Second, the divergence risk I attribute to option (a) -- that a ceiling-division count and repeated addition can differ by one spawn -- is derived from the representation of values like 0.3 and 0.1 in binary32 and I did not execute it. It informs a comparative judgement between remedies rather than a finding against anyone, and if it is wrong, option (a) is merely more expensive than option (c) rather than riskier, which does not change the ruling. Third, reachability from Studio/sim rests on reading Program.cs, and I have confirmed only that the dt values used there today are 1f/30f, 1f/60f and 1f/240f; my statement that a long-horizon sweep is a plausible future choice is a judgement about where the harness is going, not evidence, and I have labelled it as such rather than dressing it as a finding. Fourth and procedurally: this is the first challenge the studio has run end to end, so the resultingTaskId question in matter 5 -- whether a challenge may name the order it was raised against as its own corrective order -- has never been exercised against the kernel cross-checks, and I have given the fallback rather than assuming it passes.
